answer: I would like to talk about an apology that actually made a friendship stronger. I remember an occasion when a close friend apologised to me after a misunderstanding that had strained our friendship for weeks. It happened about two years ago, and the friend was someone I had known since school. We had fallen out over something fairly trivial, a comment he made about me in a group chat, which both of us had blown out of proportion. For a few weeks we barely spoke, and it felt strange not having him around, because we used to talk almost every day. Then one evening he turned up at our flat unannounced and asked if we could go for a walk by the river. What made his apology memorable was how [[sincere]] it was; he did not make excuses or try to shift the blame. He admitted openly that he had been in the wrong, which takes real [[humility]]. I think apologising properly is genuinely difficult, because it requires swallowing your pride. His honesty completely [[disarmed]] me, and any lingering resentment melted away almost instantly. In the end I apologised too, for my own stubbornness. We ended up talking for hours and our friendship actually became stronger than before. Honestly, that experience taught me how powerful a genuine apology can be in [[repairing]] a relationship. It also reminded me that admitting fault is a sign of strength, not weakness, something many people never seem to learn.

followUps.q: Do you find it easy to apologise?
followUps.answer: Not always, to be honest. Like most people, I can be a bit proud, but I have learned that a quick, genuine apology usually [[defuses]] a situation far better than defending myself.

followUps.q: Do you think people apologise less nowadays?
followUps.answer: Perhaps a little. People often send a quick sorry by message instead of saying it in person, which feels less meaningful. A face-to-face apology still carries much more weight, I think.

note: Added who he was, what the misunderstanding was, how and where he apologised (a walk by the river) and my own apology.
